title: How Many Different OR Values Do the Subarrays Have?

concept.title: For each right end there are at most 31 different ORs: extend them one by one and put them in a set
body: Take **every subarray** of the list and compute the **bitwise OR** of its elements. How many **different values** appear among all these ORs? For `1 1 2` the subarrays give `1, 1, 2, 1, 3, 3`, so the distinct values are `1, 2, 3` and the answer is 3. There are n (n + 1) / 2 subarrays, far too many to compute one by one.

The OR of a subarray can only **gain bits** when the subarray grows to the left. For a fixed right end `i`, the ORs of the subarrays that end at `i` (from the shortest to the longest) are a chain in which every value contains the bits of the previous one, so there are **at most 31 different values** per right end (the number of set bits goes from at least 1 to at most 30). Keep that small set `cur`. When the next element `x` arrives, the new set is `{v | x for v in cur}` plus the subarray `[x]` itself.

body.code:
seen = set()
cur = set()
for x in a:
    cur = {v | x for v in cur}      # extend every subarray ending at the previous element
    cur.add(x)                      # and the subarray [x]
    seen |= cur                     # all the ORs seen so far
print(len(seen))

body: Every step costs O(31), so the program is O(31 n) with set operations. The total number of values in `seen` can be close to 31 n (with sparse numbers), so memory matters; the problem limit of 20000 numbers keeps it below about 620000 values. The same method, with `&` instead of `|`, was used for counting subarrays with a given AND.

statement: A list of `n` numbers is given. For every non-empty subarray compute the bitwise OR of its elements. Print the number of distinct values among these ORs.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`: the number of values.
outputFormat: Print the number of distinct OR values.

examples.note: The ORs are 1, 1, 2, 1, 3, 3; the distinct values are 1, 2, 3: 3.

hints: For a fixed right end the OR values grow as the subarray extends to the left.
There are at most 31 distinct values per right end.
Keep the set of ORs ending at the previous element, OR each of them with the new element, and add the element itself.

explanation: For every right end the distinct ORs of the subarrays ending there (at most 31) are kept in a set; the new element is ORed into each of them, the element itself is added, and everything is collected into one global set whose size is printed.
solution.complexity: Time O(31 n) with hashing (O(31 n log n) with sorting), space O(31 n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

seen = set()
cur = set()
for x in a:
    cur = {v | x for v in cur}
    cur.add(x)
    seen |= cur
print(len(seen))
